title: Analyzing and Rewarding Credit Card Spending Habits in India: a Machine Learning Approach
authors: Agrawal, R.; Khanna, A.; Hamdare, S.
venue: International Journal of Computational Intelligence Systems
tldr: K-Means clustering and a multi-factor reward formula segment Indian credit card users and optimize reward allocation using synthetic data.
problem_and_motivation: Traditional credit card reward programs use one-size-fits-all structures that fail to personalize incentives, leading to missed opportunities to engage high-value customers. Existing ML models for spending prediction are static, struggle to generalize to high-value segments, and overlook discretionary spending categories such as luxury and travel. There is a gap in developing tailored, adaptive reward systems for the Indian credit card market.
approach: K-Means clustering segments users by card type (Platinum, Gold, Silver, Signature) based on spending behavior features including monthly spend, transactions per month, and credit utilization.

A synthetic credit card dataset is generated using Faker to overcome limitations of the original dataset, incorporating 15 attributes including income category, attrition risk, and card promotion date.
A multi-factor reward formula calculates scored points from card type multiplier, promotion bonus, expense type bonus, income category, number of cards penalty, and attrition risk bonus.
ML models (Linear Regression, XGBoost, Random Forest) validate the reward formula by independently predicting reward points from transaction features.
DBSCAN and Gaussian Mixture Models are evaluated alongside K-Means using Silhouette Scores and Davies-Bouldin Index to confirm card type as the best clustering factor.
findings: num: K-Means achieved a Silhouette Score of 0.42, outperforming DBSCAN, Hierarchical, and GMM clustering techniques.
num: Random Forest and XGBoost models achieved an R2 value of 0.99, indicating near-perfect fit to the synthetic dataset.
num: Random Forest outperformed Linear Regression and XGBoost on RMSE and MAE, making it the most accurate model for reward prediction.
num: Synthetic dataset reward points range from 0 to 3500, compared to a maximum of 1000 in the original dataset.
num: Mean reward points increased to approximately 1000 with the synthetic dataset, highlighting improved distribution fairness.
Card type clustering effectively segregates spending behaviors across Platinum (luxury/travel), Gold (balanced), Silver (essential), and Signature (routine) profiles.
Monthly spending trends show increases during festive seasons such as Diwali, Christmas, and Holi, supporting the case for seasonal reward incentives.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper contributes a multi-factor reward calculation framework for credit card spending analysis that incorporates six weighted variables beyond simple transaction amounts. It demonstrates that card type-based K-Means clustering effectively segments users into distinct spending profiles, with Silhouette Score of 0.42 validating the segmentation approach. The synthetic dataset generation methodology enables scalable testing of reward formulas when real transaction data is unavailable, and the ML validation approach (R2 of 0.99) provides a systematic method for evaluating reward formula accuracy.
directly_justifies: K-Means clustering with card type features achieves meaningful user segmentation for financial behavioral profiling.
Expense type bonuses of +3.0 for travel and +2.0 for luxury incentivize discretionary spending over essential purchases.
Attrition risk factor of +1.0 in the reward formula provides a mechanism to retain at-risk customers.
Synthetic data with 15 features produces reward distributions 3.5 times broader than the original 5-feature dataset.
Random Forest achieves R2 of 0.99 for predicting reward points from spending behavior features.
limits: The synthetic dataset is generated rather than derived from real transactions, limiting generalizability to actual credit card behavior.
The study uses only Indian credit card data, and cultural spending patterns may not transfer across markets.
No comparison against baseline reward allocation methods to quantify improvement over existing systems.
The reward formula multipliers are described as arbitrary and not derived from empirical optimization.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains were systematically scanned. High relevance was assigned to expense categorization (3.A), existing personal finance systems (4.A), limitations of those systems (4.B), financial behavioral profiles (5.A), classification approaches (5.C), engagement dynamics (11.A), retention mechanisms (11.B), and synthetic data generation (14.A). Medium relevance was assigned to predictive modeling (6.A) as the paper uses ML models but the primary contribution is the reward formula rather than novel prediction methods. Contextual relevance was assigned to financial behavior (1.C) as the paper analyzes spending behavior but not specific to Filipino young professionals. Low relevance was assigned to data privacy (10.A) which is mentioned only in passing. Topics rejected include mobile-first design (9.A-9.C), budgeting strategies (7.A-7.D), savings and debt management (13.A-13.C), and anomaly detection (8.A-8.C) as the paper does not address these domains. The paper's topical coverage centers on credit card reward optimization through clustering, synthetic data, and engagement design.
